name: Atovaquone/Proguanil

fields.mechanism_of_action: MALARONE is a fixed-dose combination of two antimalarial agents, atovaquone and proguanil hydrochloride, that interfere with two different pathways in the biosynthesis of pyrimidines required for nucleic acid replication. Atovaquone is a selective inhibitor of parasite mitochondrial electron transport. Proguanil hydrochloride primarily exerts its effect through its metabolite cycloguanil, a dihydrofolate reductase inhibitor; inhibition of dihydrofolate reductase in the Plasmodium parasite disrupts deoxythymidylate synthesis. Atovaquone and cycloguanil are active against the erythrocytic and exoerythrocytic stages of P. falciparum, and the combination is more effective than either component alone (FDA MALARONE label, sections 12.1 and 12.4).
indications: Prophylaxis of Plasmodium falciparum malaria, including in areas where chloroquine resistance has been reported (FDA MALARONE label, section 1.1).

Treatment of acute, uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria; MALARONE has been shown to be effective in regions where chloroquine, halofantrine, mefloquine and amodiaquine may have unacceptable failure rates, presumably due to drug resistance (FDA MALARONE label, section 1.2).

Kenya: listed in the Kenya Essential Medicines List 2023 under section 7.5.3.2 'For Prophylaxis' as Atovaquone + Proguanil, film-coated tablets 62.5 mg (HCl) + 25 mg and 250 mg (HCl) + 100 mg, both at Level of Use (LoU) 4; the Kenya National Medicines Formulary 2023 monograph lists the adult indication as 'Prophylaxis of falciparum malaria, particularly where resistance to other antimalarial drugs suspected' (KEML 2023, section 7.5.3.2.1; KNMF 2023, section 7.5.3.2).
contraindications: Known hypersensitivity reaction to atovaquone, proguanil hydrochloride or any component of the formulation (FDA MALARONE label, section 4).

Prophylaxis of P. falciparum malaria in patients with severe renal impairment (creatinine clearance less than 30 mL/min), because of pancytopenia reported in patients with severe renal impairment treated with proguanil (FDA MALARONE label, sections 4 and 8.6).
Patients who have developed a severe cutaneous adverse reaction (SCAR) to MALARONE must not receive it again (FDA MALARONE label, section 5.4).
side_effects: Prophylaxis, common adverse reactions (4% or more) in adults: diarrhea, dreams, oral ulcers and headache; these occurred in a similar or lower proportion of subjects receiving MALARONE than an active comparator (FDA MALARONE label, section 6.1).
Prophylaxis, common adverse reactions (5% or more) in paediatric patients: abdominal pain, headache, cough and vomiting (FDA MALARONE label, section 6.1).
Treatment, common adverse reactions (5% or more) in adolescents and adults: abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, headache, diarrhea, asthenia, anorexia and dizziness (FDA MALARONE label, section 6.1).
Treatment, common adverse reactions (6% or more) in paediatric patients: vomiting, pruritus and diarrhea (FDA MALARONE label, section 6.1).

Vomiting occurred in up to 19% of paediatric patients given treatment doses of MALARONE; in the controlled clinical trials 15.3% of adults received an antiemetic when they received atovaquone/proguanil and 98.3% of these patients were successfully treated (FDA MALARONE label, section 5.1).
Hepatobiliary: elevated liver laboratory tests, hepatitis, cholestasis, and hepatic failure requiring transplant (FDA MALARONE label, sections 5.3 and 6.2).
Blood and lymphatic system: neutropenia and anemia; pancytopenia in patients with severe renal impairment treated with proguanil (FDA MALARONE label, section 6.2).
Immune system: allergic reactions including anaphylaxis, angioedema, urticaria and vasculitis (FDA MALARONE label, section 6.2).

Nervous system and psychiatric: seizures and psychiatric adverse reactions such as hallucinations, depression, anxiety, panic attacks, crying, nightmares and psychotic disorders (FDA MALARONE label, section 6.2).
Skin: photosensitivity, rash, erythema multiforme, Stevens-Johnson syndrome and drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) (FDA MALARONE label, sections 5.4 and 6.2).

In a placebo-controlled paediatric prophylaxis study in Gabon, the most common treatment-emergent adverse events with MALARONE were abdominal pain (13%), headache (13%) and cough (10%); abdominal pain (13% vs 8%) and vomiting (5% vs 3%) were reported more often than with placebo (FDA MALARONE label, section 6.1).

dosage.adult: Prophylaxis: one MALARONE adult-strength tablet (250 mg atovaquone / 100 mg proguanil hydrochloride) once daily, started 1 or 2 days before entering a malaria-endemic area, continued daily during the stay and for 7 days after return. Treatment of acute uncomplicated malaria: four adult-strength tablets (total daily dose 1 g atovaquone / 400 mg proguanil hydrochloride) as a single daily dose for 3 consecutive days. Take the daily dose at the same time each day with food or a milky drink; if vomiting occurs within 1 hour after dosing, repeat the dose (FDA MALARONE label, sections 2, 2.1 and 2.2). Kenya: 1 tablet of 250 mg (HCl) + 100 mg once daily for prophylaxis of falciparum malaria, started 1-2 days before entering the endemic area and continued for 1 week after leaving (KEML 2023, section 7.5.3.2.1; KNMF 2023, section 7.5.3.2).
dosage.geriatric: Clinical trials of MALARONE did not include sufficient numbers of subjects aged 65 years and older to determine whether they respond differently from younger subjects. In general, dose selection for an elderly patient should be cautious, reflecting the greater frequency of decreased hepatic, renal or cardiac function, the higher systemic exposure to cycloguanil, and the greater frequency of concomitant disease or other drug therapy (FDA MALARONE label, section 8.5).
dosage.paediatric: Prophylaxis, by body weight: 11-20 kg 62.5 mg/25 mg (1 pediatric tablet daily); 21-30 kg 125 mg/50 mg (2 pediatric tablets as a single daily dose); 31-40 kg 187.5 mg/75 mg (3 pediatric tablets as a single daily dose); greater than 40 kg 250 mg/100 mg (1 adult-strength tablet as a single daily dose). Treatment, by body weight for 3 consecutive days: 5-8 kg 125 mg/50 mg (2 pediatric tablets daily); 9-10 kg 187.5 mg/75 mg (3 pediatric tablets daily); 11-20 kg 250 mg/100 mg (1 adult-strength tablet daily); 21-30 kg 500 mg/200 mg (2 adult-strength tablets as a single daily dose); 31-40 kg 750 mg/300 mg (3 adult-strength tablets as a single daily dose); greater than 40 kg 1 g/400 mg (4 adult-strength tablets as a single daily dose). Safety and effectiveness have not been established in paediatric patients who weigh less than 11 kg for prophylaxis, or less than 5 kg for treatment (FDA MALARONE label, sections 2.1, 2.2 and 8.4).

interactions: Rifampin or rifabutin: concomitant administration reduces atovaquone concentrations (by approximately 50% and 34% respectively); the concomitant administration of MALARONE with rifampin or rifabutin is not recommended (FDA MALARONE label, sections 7.1 and 12.3).

Warfarin and other coumarin-based anticoagulants: proguanil may potentiate the anticoagulant effect; the mechanism has not been established. Caution is advised when initiating or withdrawing MALARONE in patients on continuous treatment with coumarin-based anticoagulants, and coagulation tests should be closely monitored (FDA MALARONE label, section 7.2).

Tetracycline: concomitant treatment has been associated with an approximately 40% reduction in plasma concentrations of atovaquone; parasitemia should be closely monitored (FDA MALARONE label, sections 7.3 and 12.3).
Metoclopramide: metoclopramide may reduce the bioavailability of atovaquone and should be used only if other antiemetics are not available (FDA MALARONE label, sections 7.4 and 12.3).

Indinavir: concomitant administration did not change the steady-state AUC and Cmax of indinavir but decreased indinavir Ctrough by 23% (90% CI 8% to 35%); caution should be exercised when prescribing atovaquone with indinavir (FDA MALARONE label, sections 7.5 and 12.3).

CYP2C19 substrates: proguanil is metabolized primarily by CYP2C19, and potential pharmacokinetic interactions between proguanil or cycloguanil and other drugs that are CYP2C19 substrates or inhibitors are unknown (FDA MALARONE label, section 12.3).

No pharmacokinetic interactions were found between atovaquone and proguanil at the recommended dose; atovaquone is highly protein bound (>99%) but does not displace other highly protein-bound drugs in vitro (FDA MALARONE label, section 12.3).
fields.monitoring: If MALARONE is used in a patient who is vomiting, monitor parasitemia closely and consider use of an antiemetic; in patients with severe or persistent diarrhea or vomiting, alternative antimalarial therapy may be required (FDA MALARONE label, section 5.1). In mixed P. falciparum and P. vivax infection, monitor for relapse of P. vivax, which occurred commonly when patients were treated with MALARONE alone (section 5.2). If recrudescent P. falciparum infection occurs after treatment or prophylaxis failure, the patient should be treated with a different blood schizonticide (section 5.2). Monitor liver function: elevated liver laboratory tests and cases of hepatitis and hepatic failure requiring liver transplantation have been reported with prophylactic use, and patients should be advised to report jaundice, dark urine, pale stools, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, fatigue or itching (sections 5.3 and 17). Monitor for signs and symptoms of severe cutaneous adverse reactions such as rash, mucosal lesions or any other sign of hypersensitivity, and discontinue immediately if they develop (section 5.4). Closely monitor coagulation tests in patients receiving coumarin-based anticoagulants (section 7.2). Monitor parasitemia in patients receiving tetracycline concurrently (section 7.3). Obtain a platelet count and monitor for pancytopenia in patients with severe renal impairment who receive proguanil (sections 4 and 8.6).
fields.patient_counselling: Advise patients to take MALARONE at the same time each day with food or a milky drink (FDA MALARONE label, section 17). Advise patients to take a repeat dose if vomiting occurs within 1 hour after dosing (section 2 and section 17). Advise patients to take a missed dose as soon as they remember and then return to the normal dosing schedule; if a dose is skipped, the patient should not double the next dose (section 17). Advise patients about the signs and symptoms of serious skin manifestations and instruct them to stop taking MALARONE immediately and promptly report the first signs or symptoms of skin rash, mucosal lesions or any other sign of hypersensitivity (section 17). Advise patients to immediately report symptoms of hepatotoxicity such as yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine, pale stools, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, fatigue or itching (section 17). Tablets may be crushed and mixed with condensed milk just prior to administration for patients who have difficulty swallowing (section 2).
warnings: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions (SCARs) such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS), drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) and erythema multiforme (EM) have been reported and can be life-threatening or fatal; if symptoms or signs of SCARs develop, discontinue MALARONE immediately and institute appropriate therapy, and patients who have developed SCARs must not receive MALARONE again (FDA MALARONE label, section 5.4).

Atovaquone absorption may be reduced in patients with diarrhea or vomiting; parasitemia should be closely monitored and use of an antiemetic considered, and alternative antimalarial therapy may be required in patients with severe or persistent diarrhea or vomiting (FDA MALARONE label, section 5.1).
In mixed P. falciparum and P. vivax infection, P. vivax relapse occurred commonly when patients were treated with MALARONE alone (FDA MALARONE label, section 5.2).
In the event of recrudescent P. falciparum infections after treatment or prophylaxis failure, patients should be treated with a different blood schizonticide (FDA MALARONE label, section 5.2).
Elevated liver laboratory tests and cases of hepatitis and hepatic failure requiring liver transplantation have been reported with prophylactic use (FDA MALARONE label, section 5.3).

MALARONE has not been evaluated for the treatment of cerebral malaria or other severe manifestations of complicated malaria, including hyperparasitemia, pulmonary edema or renal failure; patients with severe malaria are not candidates for oral therapy (FDA MALARONE label, section 5.5).

Prophylaxis is contraindicated in patients with severe renal impairment (creatinine clearance less than 30 mL/min) because of pancytopenia in patients with severe renal impairment treated with proguanil (FDA MALARONE label, sections 4 and 8.6).
precautions: Use with caution for the treatment of malaria in patients with severe renal impairment, only if the benefits of the 3-day treatment regimen outweigh the potential risks associated with increased drug exposure; no dosage adjustments are needed in patients with mild (CrCl 50 to 80 mL/min) or moderate (CrCl 30 to 50 mL/min) renal impairment (FDA MALARONE label, sections 2.3 and 8.6).
No dosage adjustments are needed in patients with mild or moderate hepatic impairment; no trials have been conducted in patients with severe hepatic impairment (FDA MALARONE label, section 8.7).

Proguanil is metabolized to the active metabolite cycloguanil primarily via CYP2C19; people with reduced CYP2C19 activity do not effectively metabolize proguanil to cycloguanil and are effectively receiving only the chloroquine component of their therapy, with an increased risk of adverse effects, especially gastrointestinal (FDA MALARONE label, section 12.3; KNMF 2023, Proguanil monograph).

Pregnant women and females of reproductive potential should continue folate supplementation to prevent neural tube defects, because the proguanil component acts to inhibit parasitic dihydrofolate reductase (FDA MALARONE label, section 8.1).

MALARONE should be used with caution in patients with a history of neuropsychiatric disorders, and in patients with severe renal impairment for treatment of malaria, where the higher systemic exposure to cycloguanil increases the risk of adverse effects (FDA MALARONE label, sections 8.5, 8.6 and 12.3; KNMF 2023, Proguanil monograph: 'Avoid use in cardiac conduction disorders and in epilepsy'; 'Use with caution in severe renal impairment, otherwise dose reduction not needed').
serious_adverse_reactions: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions (Stevens-Johnson syndrome, DRESS, erythema multiforme), which can be life-threatening or fatal (FDA MALARONE label, sections 5.4 and 6.2)
Hepatotoxicity, including hepatitis, cholestasis and hepatic failure requiring liver transplantation (FDA MALARONE label, sections 5.3 and 6.2)
Anaphylaxis and other serious allergic reactions, including angioedema, urticaria and vasculitis (FDA MALARONE label, section 6.2)
Seizures and serious psychiatric adverse reactions, including hallucinations, depression, anxiety, panic attacks and psychotic disorders (FDA MALARONE label, section 6.2)
Pancytopenia in patients with severe renal impairment treated with proguanil (FDA MALARONE label, sections 4 and 6.2)
food_interactions: Take MALARONE with food or a milky drink. Atovaquone is a highly lipophilic compound with low aqueous solubility; dietary fat taken with atovaquone increases the rate and extent of absorption, increasing AUC 2 to 3 times and Cmax 5 times over fasting, and the absolute bioavailability of the tablet formulation of atovaquone when taken with food is 23% (FDA MALARONE label, sections 2 and 12.3).
Tablets may be crushed and mixed with condensed milk just prior to administration for patients who may have difficulty swallowing tablets (FDA MALARONE label, section 2).
fields.pregnancy_guidance: Available data from published literature and postmarketing experience with use of MALARONE in pregnant women are insufficient to identify a drug-associated risk for major birth defects, miscarriage, or adverse maternal or fetal outcomes. The proguanil component acts to inhibit parasitic dihydrofolate reductase; pregnant women and females of reproductive potential should continue folate supplementation to prevent neural tube defects. Pregnant women with malaria are at increased risk for adverse pregnancy outcomes, including maternal anemia, prematurity, spontaneous abortion and stillbirth. Atovaquone administered by oral gavage to pregnant rats and rabbits during organogenesis was not associated with fetal malformations; the combination given orally by gavage during organogenesis was not associated with embryo-fetal developmental effects in pregnant rats or rabbits at atovaquone:proguanil hydrochloride doses of 50:20 mg/kg/day and 100:40 mg/kg/day respectively. The estimated background risk of major birth defects and miscarriage in the US general population is 2% to 4% and 15% to 20% respectively (FDA MALARONE label, section 8.1). Kenya: the KNMF 2023 records 'Pregnancy: Manufacturer advises use only if potential benefit outweighs risk' (KNMF 2023, section 7.5.3.2).
fields.lactation_guidance: There are no data on the presence of atovaquone in human milk; however, proguanil is present in human milk. Atovaquone is present in rat milk (atovaquone concentrations in milk were 30% of concurrent maternal plasma concentrations at 10 and 250 mg/kg). There are no data on the effects of atovaquone and proguanil on the breastfed child or the effects on milk production. The developmental and health benefits of breastfeeding should be considered along with the mother's clinical need for MALARONE and any potential adverse effect on the breastfed child from MALARONE or from the underlying maternal condition (FDA MALARONE label, section 8.2). Kenya: the KNMF 2023 records 'Breastfeeding: Use only if no suitable alternative available' (KNMF 2023, section 7.5.3.2).
fields.overdose: There is no information on overdoses of MALARONE substantially higher than the doses recommended for treatment. There is no known antidote for atovaquone, and it is currently unknown if atovaquone is dialyzable. Overdoses up to 31,500 mg of atovaquone have been reported; in one such patient who also took an unspecified dose of dapsone, methemoglobinemia occurred, and rash has also been reported after overdose. Overdoses of proguanil hydrochloride as large as 1,500 mg have been followed by complete recovery, and doses as high as 700 mg twice daily have been taken for over 2 weeks without serious toxicity. Adverse experiences occasionally associated with proguanil hydrochloride doses of 100 to 200 mg/day, such as epigastric discomfort and vomiting, would be likely to occur with overdose. There are also reports of reversible hair loss and scaling of the skin on the palms and/or soles, reversible aphthous ulceration, and hematologic side effects (FDA MALARONE label, section 10).
fields.pharmacokinetics: Atovaquone is a highly lipophilic compound with low aqueous solubility and the bioavailability of atovaquone shows considerable inter-individual variability; the absolute bioavailability of the tablet formulation taken with food is 23%. Atovaquone is highly protein bound (>99%) over the range 1 to 90 mcg/mL, with an apparent volume of distribution (V/F) of approximately 8.8 L/kg in adult and paediatric patients. Proguanil is 75% protein bound, with an apparent V/F ranging from 1,617 to 2,502 L in adults and children older than 15 years and from 462 to 966 L in paediatric patients 15 years and younger. The elimination half-life of atovaquone is about 2 to 3 days in adult patients; the elimination half-life of proguanil is 12 to 21 hours in both adult and paediatric patients but may be longer in slow metabolizers. The main routes of elimination are hepatic biotransformation and renal excretion. Greater than 94% of a radiolabelled atovaquone dose was recovered as unchanged atovaquone in the feces over 21 days, with less than 0.6% excreted in urine; proguanil is metabolized to cycloguanil (primarily via CYP2C19) and 4-chlorophenylbiguanide, and 40% to 60% of proguanil is excreted by the kidneys (FDA MALARONE label, section 12.3).
clinical_pearls: Take the tablet with food or a milky drink: dietary fat increases atovaquone AUC 2 to 3 times and Cmax 5 times over fasting (FDA MALARONE label, sections 2 and 12.3).

If the patient vomits within 1 hour of dosing, give a repeat dose; vomiting occurred in up to 19% of paediatric patients on treatment doses and 15.3% of adults needed an antiemetic (FDA MALARONE label, sections 2 and 5.1).

MALARONE does not cover P. vivax hypnozoites: in mixed P. falciparum/P. vivax infection, P. vivax relapse occurred commonly with MALARONE alone, so radical cure of vivax/ovale needs separate antimalarial therapy (FDA MALARONE label, section 5.2).
Never use MALARONE for prophylaxis in severe renal impairment (CrCl less than 30 mL/min) - proguanil has been associated with pancytopenia in this group (FDA MALARONE label, sections 4 and 8.6).
Rifampicin and rifabutin reduce atovaquone exposure by roughly 50% and 34% respectively, so the combination is not recommended (FDA MALARONE label, sections 7.1 and 12.3).
Proguanil is activated to cycloguanil by CYP2C19; slow metabolisers effectively get only the chloroquine-like component, so efficacy and adverse-effect risk differ (FDA MALARONE label, section 12.3).
The Kenya Essential Medicines List 2023 places both strengths of atovaquone + proguanil at Level of Use (LoU) 4 for malaria chemoprophylaxis (KEML 2023, section 7.5.3.2.1).
brand_names: MALARONE (atovaquone and proguanil hydrochloride tablets, GSK)
fields.renal_dose_adjustment: Do not use MALARONE for malaria prophylaxis in patients with severe renal impairment (creatinine clearance less than 30 mL/min). Use with caution for the treatment of malaria in patients with severe renal impairment, only if the benefits of the 3-day treatment regimen outweigh the potential risks associated with increased drug exposure. No dosage adjustments are needed in patients with mild (CrCl 50 to 80 mL/min) or moderate (CrCl 30 to 50 mL/min) renal impairment (FDA MALARONE label, sections 2.3 and 8.6).
fields.hepatic_dose_adjustment: No dosage adjustments are needed in patients with mild or moderate hepatic impairment. No trials have been conducted in patients with severe hepatic impairment (FDA MALARONE label, section 8.7).
fields.administration_instructions: For oral administration. Take the daily dose at the same time each day with food or a milky drink. Start prophylaxis 1 or 2 days before entering a malaria-endemic area, continue daily during the stay and for 7 days after return. For treatment, take four adult-strength tablets as a single daily dose for 3 consecutive days. If vomiting occurs within 1 hour after dosing, take a repeat dose. If a dose is missed, take it as soon as remembered and then return to the normal schedule; do not double the next dose. MALARONE may be crushed and mixed with condensed milk just prior to administration for patients who may have difficulty swallowing tablets. Store at 20 to 25 degrees C (68 to 77 degrees F) in the original package, protect from moisture and light, and do not store above 30 degrees C (86 degrees F) (FDA MALARONE label, sections 2, 16 and 17). Kenya: film-coated tablets 62.5 mg (HCl) + 25 mg and 250 mg (HCl) + 100 mg (KEML 2023, section 7.5.3.2.1; KNMF 2023, section 7.5.3.2).

notes: The table stores this agent as 'Atovaquone/Proguanil'. The FDA label for MALARONE (GSK) is the primary source: adult-strength tablets 250 mg atovaquone / 100 mg proguanil hydrochloride and pediatric tablets 62.5 mg / 25 mg. Kenya context: the Kenya Essential Medicines List 2023 lists Atovaquone + Proguanil (film-coated tablets 62.5 mg + 25 mg and 250 mg + 100 mg) at Level of Use (LoU) 4 for malaria chemoprophylaxis, and the Kenya National Medicines Formulary 2023 (KNMF-1) carries a full monograph including the LOU 4 designation and the CYP2C19/cycloguanil caveat. Atovaquone monotherapy (MEPRON) is a different product and is not covered here. WHO Model List status: proguanil was first added to the WHO Model List in 1979 (TRS 641) and was removed in 2025 (TRS 1064) for malaria due to P. falciparum; atovaquone is not itself listed on the WHO Model List, so the WHO eEML is cited only for that status note and the core clinical content is FDA-label based. There is no boxed warning for MALARONE.
